reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A pterygium is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of conjunctival tissue that encroaches onto the cornea, most commonly on the nasal side
Strongly associated with chronic exposure to ultraviolet light, wind, and dust, and therefore more common in people living in sunny, outdoor environments near the equator
It is distinguished from a pinguecula, which is a similar degenerative conjunctival lesion that does not cross onto the cornea
Symptoms range from a cosmetic concern and irritation or redness to visual disturbance when it induces astigmatism or approaches the visual axis
A leading edge (Stocker's line of iron deposition) and a fibrovascular head advancing over the cornea are characteristic
Management is conservative with lubricants and UV protection for mild lesions; surgical excision is indicated for visual axis threat, marked astigmatism, discomfort, or cosmesis
Recurrence after excision is common, and adjuncts such as conjunctival autografting reduce this risk compared with bare-scleral excision
Atypical or rapidly growing lesions should be evaluated to exclude ocular surface squamous neoplasia
reference.pathophysiology: A pterygium is a degenerative and proliferative condition of the bulbar conjunctiva in which chronic ultraviolet and environmental exposure causes elastotic degeneration of subepithelial collagen along with fibrovascular proliferation. The abnormal tissue invades the superficial cornea, disrupting Bowman's layer and the corneal architecture at its advancing head. Progressive growth can flatten the cornea and induce astigmatism, and encroachment onto the visual axis reduces vision.
additionalDifferentials: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia)
Conjunctival naevus or other pigmented lesion
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to document size, vascularity, and encroachment onto the cornea
Refraction and corneal topography to assess induced astigmatism
Excision biopsy with histology when ocular surface neoplasia is suspected
redFlags: Rapid growth, marked thickening, or leukoplakic change suggesting ocular surface squamous neoplasia
Encroachment onto or across the visual axis threatening vision
Restricted ocular motility from a large or recurrent lesion with scarring
reference.prognosis: Most pterygia are benign and slowly progressive with a good prognosis; surgery is effective for symptomatic or vision-threatening lesions, though recurrence is a recognised problem, particularly with bare-scleral techniques and in younger patients.
pitfalls: Assuming all fleshy conjunctival lesions are benign pterygia and missing ocular surface neoplasia
Operating too early on quiescent lesions given the risk of recurrence
Using bare-scleral excision alone, which has a high recurrence rate compared with grafting
Neglecting UV protection advice, allowing progression or recurrence
management: Ocular lubricants and, for inflamed lesions, short courses of topical corticosteroids or decongestants to relieve irritation and redness
Ultraviolet protection with sunglasses and brimmed hats and avoidance of wind and dust exposure to slow progression
Surgical excision for lesions threatening the visual axis, inducing marked astigmatism, or causing troublesome symptoms or cosmetic concern
Conjunctival autograft rather than a bare-scleral technique, or adjunctive mitomycin C, to reduce recurrence after excision
Refraction and corneal topography to quantify induced astigmatism, with serial slit-lamp examination and photography to monitor growth
Histological examination of excised tissue to exclude ocular surface squamous neoplasia in atypical lesions
Ophthalmology referral for symptomatic or progressive lesions
